rationale: The data come from four CSF cohorts, and each cohort has its own protein-level offsets from pre-analytics and acquisition. The current model learns one set of weights on the pooled data, so those cohort offsets mix with the disease signal. Since scoring is within site, I'll subtract each protein's per-site median (computed without labels in `featurize`). This harmonizes the cohorts before fitting and should let the L2 logistic regression focus on within-site differences between AD and non-AD.

CSF studies (Bader 2020, Higginbotham/Johnson 2020) consistently report a small set of proteins that rise in AD alongside tau: SMOC1, the 14-3-3 proteins, glycolytic enzymes, SPP1 and CHI3L1. With n≈110 per training fold, an L2 model over ~1,000 proteins has a hard time finding this signal. So I'm adding a label-free prior score: the mean training-standardized abundance of that "up in AD" panel, rank-averaged equally with the existing logistic regression. The panel and its sign come from prior biology, so the score adds no extra fitted parameters.

I'm making the prior-biology module two-sided. It currently averages only the tau-linked proteins that rise in AD. It will now also subtract the mean of synaptic/neurosecretory proteins that consistently fall in clinical AD CSF: NPTX2, NPTXR, NPTX1, VGF, SCG2 and NRN1 (Higginbotham 2020, Johnson 2022). The two groups move in opposite directions, so their difference should separate AD from non-AD better than either group alone. Both panels and their signs come from the literature, so nothing new is fitted to labels.

The fixed 50/50 rank average of the logistic regression and the two-sided module is arbitrary. I'll choose the module's blend weight from {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1} by grouped inner CV on the training fold. The inner CV scores within-site AUROC, the same metric the harness uses, and ties go to the weight closest to 0.5. The module has no fitted parameters and is probably the more reliable signal at this small n, so the data should decide how much the noisier model gets to dilute it.

CSF samples carry different amounts of blood contamination, and many proteins in the AD-up panel (GAPDH, ENO1, PKM, ALDOA, LDHB, TPI1, PGK1, PPIA, the 14-3-3 proteins) are also very abundant in red blood cells (Geyer et al. 2019 contamination panels). That contamination adds noise to both the module score and the logistic regression. This change builds a label-free contamination score from red-cell-specific proteins (hemoglobins, CA1/CA2, CAT, PRDX2, …), using training samples only. It then removes each protein's linear dependence on that score before standardizing.

Low-abundance markers like MAPT, NEFL, GFAP, ENO2 and NPTX1 are quantified in fewer than 70% of CSF samples, so the global filter drops them and they never reach the module. Their values are probably missing because the protein fell below detection, so a low value or a missing one is itself evidence of how much is there. This change keeps panel proteins seen in at least 25% of training samples and fills their gaps at half-minimum. They feed only the prior-biology module; the logistic regression keeps the stricter 70% set.

Scoring is within each site, but the LR and module scores are currently converted to ranks across the whole multi-site test fold. Each component's site offsets therefore change how many rank steps it spans inside a given site, so the effective 50/50 weight varies by site. I'll rank each component within its own test site (site used only for harmonization) before averaging, so both get equal weight inside every cohort.

The down-in-AD side of the module averages only about six proteins, while the up side has many more, so the down side is the noisier half. I'm adding the other neurosecretory dense-core-vesicle proteins (chromogranins CHGA and CHGB, secretogranins SCG3 and SCG5, and PCSK1N). These are co-released with VGF and SCG2 and form the same CSF synaptic/neurosecretory module, which is reported as decreased in clinical AD (Jahn 2011, Duits 2018, Higginbotham 2020). Averaging more members of that module should make the down score less noisy, and nothing new is fitted to labels.

CSF samples differ in how much plasma protein crosses the blood–CSF barrier (the CSF/serum albumin quotient varies 2–3-fold between people, mostly with age and vascular factors rather than AD). That shared plasma-leakage factor shifts the median normalization and adds noise to every brain-derived protein. I'll extend the kept erythrocyte correction to fit both a red-cell index and a plasma-leakage index together. The plasma index uses blood-derived proteins: albumin, apolipoproteins A1/A2/B, haptoglobin, fibrinogens, A2M, AHSG, ITIHs, immunoglobulins and others. The fit uses training-fold slopes only and no labels, so both the LR and the module see brain-specific variation.

I'm making the up-in-AD side of the module larger, the same way round 8 enlarged the down side. I'm adding more members of the CSF glycolysis/14-3-3 module that rises with tau (ALDOC, PGAM1, LDHA, CD44; Higginbotham 2020, Johnson 2023), plus synaptic-injury markers that rise in AD CSF more than in other neurological diseases (NRGN, GAP43, SNAP25, SYT1). Averaging more members of the module should make the up score less noisy. The signs come from the literature, nothing new is fitted to labels, and any added protein that fails the 70% filter is simply left out. I haven't run this, so I don't know the new score yet.

Right now the module averages every panel protein with equal weight, so the nine glycolytic enzymes control most of the up side. Those enzymes are also the proteins most exposed to red-cell contamination, and round 10 got worse when more of them were added. I'll average proteins within each biological sub-module first (SMOC1/SPP1 matrisome, 14-3-3, glycolysis, glial, neuronal injury; pentraxin/synaptic, dense-core-vesicle granins), then average the sub-modules with equal weight. That way the strongest specific markers (SMOC1, SPP1, the 14-3-3 proteins, the pentraxins) are not drowned out by one large correlated group, and nothing new is fitted to labels.

The four cohorts probably have different AD/non-AD ratios, so the pooled L2 logistic regression can treat proteins that mark a cohort as AD predictors. That cannot help when scoring is within site. I'll weight training samples by 1/count(site, class) so that, in the weighted loss, every cohort is class-balanced and site carries no information about the label. Site is used only to harmonize the training objective, and the module and nuisance correction stay unchanged.

The L2 logistic regression currently penalizes every one of about 1,000 proteins equally. At n≈110, that spreads the weight over many noisy proteins and lets the literature AD markers be shrunk away. I'll multiply the standardized columns of the up-in-AD and down-in-AD panel proteins by 2 before fitting the LR. That gives those proteins a 4× wider Gaussian prior on their coefficients, so the LR leans toward known biology while staying free to learn the panels' weights and signs and to use other proteins. The module and nuisance correction stay unchanged.

The two halves of the module, the mean z of the up-in-AD proteins and the mean z of the down-in-AD proteins, share a common factor: how much brain-derived protein ends up in the CSF, which depends on CSF turnover and dilution. Taking their difference cancels that factor, but only if both halves are on the same scale. Right now the more tightly correlated half has the larger variance, so the cancellation is lopsided. I will standardize each half by its training-fold SD (no labels used) before subtracting, so both halves carry equal weight and the shared factor cancels more cleanly.

Right now each sample's median is taken over whichever proteins happen to be quantified. Missing values are not random: in samples with weaker signal, low-abundance proteins drop out, which pushes the median up. The offset subtracted from every protein then depends on detection depth rather than on how much protein the sample contains. I'll compute each sample's median only from proteins quantified in at least 95% of samples (falling back to 90% or 80% if that leaves fewer than 50), so every sample is centred on almost the same reference proteins. This uses no labels.

Adding the granins to the down side of the module helped in round 8, so I'm adding the rest of the dense-core-vesicle neurosecretory pathway to the down-in-AD panel. That means neuropeptide precursors (SST, PENK, PDYN, TAC1, CCK, NPY, CARTPT, CRH) and the enzymes that process them (CPE, PCSK2, PAM). Lower CSF somatostatin and other neuropeptides is a long-standing finding in clinical AD, and these proteins are co-released with VGF/SCG2. Averaging more members of the same module should make the noisier down side less noisy. Nothing new is fitted to labels, and any protein that fails the 70% filter is simply left out. I haven't run this, so I don't know the new score yet.

After the erythrocyte and plasma-leakage indices are regressed out, the proteins that define those indices (hemoglobins, CA1/2, albumin, apolipoproteins, fibrinogens and so on) keep only small residuals. Those residuals are measurement noise with no brain-derived AD biology, but StandardScaler blows them back up to unit variance, so the n≈110 logistic regression can fit noise on about 50 extra columns. This change drops the nuisance-panel proteins from the logistic regression's features. They are still used to build the indices, and the module is unchanged.

Immunoglobulins in CSF come from two sources: transfer across the blood–CSF barrier, and synthesis inside the CNS. Intrathecal synthesis is common in the inflammatory and other neurological diseases in the clinical non-AD group. With IgG/IgA/IgM/IgKC in the plasma-leakage panel, the index (meant as an albumin-quotient analogue) picks up that immune signal, and the regression then strips it from every protein. This change drops the immunoglobulins from the plasma panel, so the index reflects barrier leakage more purely, and the immunoglobulins go back into the logistic regression as ordinary features that may carry diagnostic signal.

Rounds 10 and 16 suggest the added candidates (APOE, CLU, complement, glial and synaptic-injury markers, neuropeptides, APP family) hurt the fixed-sign module because their direction and size are inconsistent across studies. This change adds them to the logistic regression only, with a moderately wider coefficient prior (1.5× column scale, between the core panels' 2× and the 1× for other proteins), so the model learns their weight and sign; the module is unchanged.

The fixed-sign module currently treats CHI3L1, GFAP and NEFL as markers that rise in AD. These are general glial and axonal injury markers, and they are often just as high or higher in the clinical non-AD group (MS and other neuroinflammatory conditions, FTD, vascular or ALS-spectrum disease), so they should not separate clinical AD from non-AD. I'm taking them out of the module, which leaves only the AD-specific proteins: tau-related, 14-3-3, glycolysis and SMOC1/SPP1. The logistic regression keeps them with the same wider coefficient prior, so it can still learn their weight and sign from the data.
